content: If an electrical circuit has a clearly defined output terminal, the circuit connected to this terminal, or its input impedance, is referred to as the load. The term load can also describe the power consumed by the circuit, but that aspect is not addressed here. The load significantly influences the performance of circuits that output voltages or currents, such as sensors, voltage sources, and amplifiers. A simple example can be observed in household power outlets. These outlets act as voltage sources, providing, for instance, 120V AC in the United States. The collective appliances in the household represent the load. When a high-power appliance is turned on, it substantially reduces the load impedance, which in turn causes the output voltage to drop. This voltage drop is noticeable; for example, turning on a vacuum cleaner may cause the lights to dim. For a more technical perspective, two points should be noted for advanced readers: this discussion will disregard nonlinearity and will use simple resistances, which can be generalized to impedances for AC analysis. When analyzing the effect of a load on a circuit, it is often useful to ignore the specific design of the circuit and instead consider its Thévenin equivalent. (The Norton equivalent could also be used, but this explanation will focus on the Thévenin form.) The Thévenin equivalent of a circuit can be described as follows: when there is no load (i.e., the output terminals are open-circuited), the entire source voltage, ( V_S ), appears across the output terminals, and the output voltage equals ( V_S ). However, the behavior of the circuit changes when a load is introduced. To simplify the analysis, the details of the load circuit can be ignored, and the load can be represented as an input resistance. When the load is represented by an input resistance, the complete circuit can be visualized as follows: initially, the voltage source alone forms an open circuit. Adding the load creates a closed circuit, allowing current to flow. This current generates a voltage drop across the source resistance, ( R_S ), which means the voltage at the output terminal is no longer equal to ( V_S ).
